plan.chapter_thesis: The central bottleneck in metasurface holography is the uncoupled treatment of design, fabrication, and modulation, which necessitates a shift toward co-design frameworks that jointly optimize physical device geometry with computational algorithms and manufacturing constraints.
plan.reader_takeaway: Future progress in metasurface holography depends not on isolated improvements in inverse design or fabrication, but on integrated co-design strategies that resolve the trade-offs between optical performance, manufacturability, and system-level functionality.

argument_sequence.purpose: Establish the computational dominance of deep learning and inverse design in navigating high-dimensional metasurface spaces, while identifying the fundamental ill-posed nature of the problem.
Contrast heuristic and black-box methods with physics-informed approaches, arguing that integrating domain knowledge is essential for physical consistency and generalizability.
Detail specific advanced algorithmic architectures (tandem networks, diffusion models, adjoint methods) that address non-uniqueness and accelerate convergence.
Analyze the bifurcation of optimization strategies between gradient-based and gradient-free methods, highlighting the trade-off between speed and global optimality.
Identify the 'coupled mechanism bottleneck' where geometric and propagation phases interact, creating complex optimization landscapes that simple inverse design cannot solve alone.
Introduce co-design frameworks that integrate fabrication tolerance and physical constraints directly into the loss function to bridge the simulation-to-experiment gap.
Expand the scope to end-to-end system co-design, where metasurfaces are optimized jointly with downstream computational algorithms and hybrid refractive elements.
Synthesize emerging physical principles (BICs, nonlocal effects) and multi-physics techniques that offer pathways to break current trade-off triangles.

terminology_rows.note: Computational approach mapping target optical responses to structural parameters using optimization or ML.
Integration of governing equations (e.g., Maxwell's) into ML loss functions to ensure physical validity.
The phenomenon where distinct meta-atom geometries yield identical optical properties, complicating inverse mapping.
Joint optimization of device geometry, fabrication constraints, and system-level algorithms.
High-Q resonant states used to enhance light-matter interaction and efficiency.
Gradient-based optimization technique for efficient calculation of sensitivities in complex geometries.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Computational Imperative and the Ill-Posed Nature of Inverse Design
explanation_block_rows.goal: Establish that while deep learning enables exploration of vast design spaces, the fundamental non-uniqueness of metasurface mappings creates an ill-posed problem requiring specialized solutions.

explanation_block_rows.title: From Heuristics to Physics-Informed Constraints
explanation_block_rows.goal: Argue that purely data-driven or heuristic methods fail due to physical inconsistencies, necessitating the integration of domain knowledge and explicit constraints.

explanation_block_rows.title: Advanced Architectures for Non-Uniqueness and Convergence
explanation_block_rows.goal: Detail how specific deep learning architectures (tandem, residual, diffusion) and adjoint methods technically resolve the non-uniqueness and speed bottlenecks.

explanation_block_rows.title: Optimization Paradigms: Speed versus Global Optimality
explanation_block_rows.goal: Contrast gradient-based and gradient-free approaches, explaining the trade-offs in navigating nonconvex, high-dimensional parameter spaces.
